text.text: <atomic>Mia has two small ponds on her farm. She noticed that one pond was growing algae while the other was not.</atomic>
<atomic>She wondered what could be causing the difference in algae growth in her ponds.</atomic>
<atomic>She predicted that one pond was growing more algae because it received more runoff when it rained.</atomic>
<atomic>To test this, Mia dug a small ravine to catch runoff, ensuring that it didn't flow into either pond. After one month, she reassessed the algae growth.</atomic>
<atomic>She found that the algae growths had not changed; one pond was still growing more algae than the other.</atomic>
<atomic>Mia thought that since one pond was in direct sunlight, the sunlight may be killing algae growths.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Harry was helping his younger sister use a foam dart launcher that she received for her birthday.</atomic>
<atomic>They wondered what launch angle would cause the foam dart to travel the farthest horizontally.</atomic>

<atomic>They thought that launching with a higher angle to the ground would give the dart more time to travel before hitting the ground and would therefore allow the foam dart to travel farther.</atomic>

<atomic>Harry and his sister set up an experiment in their backyard. They used a protractor to adjust the launcher to five different angles: 15°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 75°. They launched three foam darts from each angle and used a measuring tape to determine how far each dart traveled horizontally.</atomic>

<atomic>They then calculated the average for each group and graphed the results. They found that the darts launched at 45° went the farthest, while those launched at 15° and 75° traveled the shortest distance.</atomic>
<atomic>Harry and his sister shared their results with the friend who had given his sister the launcher.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Sue watched boats on the river.</atomic>
<atomic>She noticed that some of the boats were V-shaped, and other boats seemed to have flat bottoms.</atomic>
<atomic>She speculated that the shape of the boat bottom might affect how much weight the boat could hold, so that flat-bottomed boats would hold more weight.</atomic>
<atomic>So, she decided to make several aluminum foil boats to float in the bathtub.</atomic>
<atomic>She made ten boats with flat bottoms and ten boats with V-shaped bottoms, and then she kept track of the number of pennies it took to sink each boat in the water.</atomic>
<atomic>Sue compared the average number of pennies it took to sink the boats in each of the two groups.</atomic>
<atomic>Because the flat-bottomed boats held more pennies, she reasoned that the shape of the boat bottom affected how much weight the boat could hold.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Eddie likes to make rock candy to share with his friends.</atomic>
<atomic>He normally makes rock candy using white sugar but wondered if he could make larger sugar crystals using pure cane sugar.</atomic>
<atomic>He predicted that pure cane sugar would make the largest crystals, since it was a more pure form of sugar.</atomic>

<atomic>Eddie set up 12 glass jars with a stick and hot water. He added white sugar to 6 jars and pure cane sugar to the other 6. After one week, Eddie measured the size of the sugar crystals in each jar.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that the rock candy made with white sugar had larger crystals than those made with pure cane sugar.</atomic>
<atomic>He then predicted that smaller sugar granules would lead to larger sugar crystals.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Philip loves hot chocolate. Last winter, he often made it by warming a pot of milk on the stove and then stirring in the powdery hot chocolate mix.</atomic>
<atomic>When the weather got warmer, Philip wondered if the mix would dissolve in milk from the refrigerator so that he could make a refreshing new drink: cold chocolate.</atomic>

<atomic>To test his idea, Philip poured nine cups of milk. He put three in the fridge, left three out on the counter, and warmed up the last three. When all the cups reached their correct temperatures, he stirred a tablespoon of hot chocolate mix into each of them.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that the hot milk dissolved the most mix, while the cold milk dissolved the least.</atomic>
<atomic>Philip now thought that milk must be warm to dissolve the mix well.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Smithfield City's landfill was almost full. To cut down on garbage, the city council decided to give residents compost bins for their food scraps.</atomic>
<atomic>That way, composted food would decompose, or break down into soil, and there would be less garbage going to the landfill.</atomic>
<atomic>One city council member, Sally, knew that worms help with decomposition, so she thought the food would decompose faster if they added worms to the bins.</atomic>
<atomic>She set up twenty different compost bins, half with worms and half without. After one month, she measured the percentage of food left in each bin.</atomic>
<atomic>Sally found that the bins with worms had less undecomposed food left, so she concluded that worms helped decompose the food scraps faster.</atomic>
<atomic>She informed the other city council members of her results and conclusions.</atomic>
<atomic>The city council decided to give out worms with the compost bins.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Amy tends to a community herb garden. She heard from a colleague that plants need nitrogen to grow.</atomic>
<atomic>She wondered if adding a nitrogen-based fertilizer to the soil would increase the growth rate of her herbs.</atomic>
<atomic>Amy added a nitrogen-based fertilizer to the soil of half the herbs and left the other half unchanged. After one month, she measured the height of all of the herbs.</atomic>
<atomic>She found that the herbs without fertilizer grew to an average height of 6 inches, while the herbs with fertilizer grew to an average height of 10 inches.</atomic>
<atomic>Amy concluded that nitrogen-based fertilizer increases the rate at which herbs grow.</atomic>
<atomic>Amy shared her findings with her colleagues at the community garden.</atomic>

<atomic>Sophie found that the balloon she'd rubbed against wool stuck to the wall, just like the one she'd rubbed against her hair. The other balloons did not.</atomic>
<atomic>She deduced that the wool had transferred more charge to the balloon than the other materials had.</atomic>
<atomic>She showed a friend her trick to get the balloon to stick to the wall and shared her findings about the different materials.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>To introduce color theory, Ian's science teacher gave each lab group three colored bulbs: one blue, one green, and one red. She instructed the groups to predict what colors the bulbs' lights would make when mixed.</atomic>

<atomic>Ian's group reasoned that the colors should mix just like paint—red and green would make brown, blue and red would make purple, blue and green would make teal, and all three would make a dark brownish color.</atomic>
<atomic>To test their predictions, Ian and his group shined their bulbs on the wall so that the colored light overlapped.</atomic>
<atomic>The resulting colors were not what the group had expected. Red and green made yellow, blue and green made cyan, blue and red made magenta, and all three made white!</atomic>
<atomic>They decided that they were wrong, and that colored bulbs must be different from paint.</atomic>
<atomic>All the groups shared their results, and their teacher explained that paint absorbs certain colors of light and reflects others, while bulbs produce certain colors of light.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Lester took his motorized toy boat to the park with his cousin.</atomic>
<atomic>The boat zipped across the pond, and Lester wondered if adding mass to the boat would affect its speed.</atomic>
<atomic>He didn't think so, since the motor should keep propelling it at the same rate.</atomic>

<atomic>Lester decided to time the boat as it traveled from one side of the pond to the other. He then taped a pebble to the boat and timed it again. Finally, he added a second pebble and repeated the procedure.</atomic>
<atomic>Lester noticed that as he added mass, the trips took longer. The empty boat took the least time to cross the pond, and the boat with two pebbles took the longest.</atomic>
<atomic>Lester concluded that adding mass does slow down the boat.</atomic>
<atomic>He changed his prediction: The motor must provide a set amount of force, so it can't maintain the same speed as more mass is added.</atomic>
<atomic>He shared his results with his aunt and confirmed that the boat's motor exerts a consistent force, so increasing the boat's mass reduces its acceleration.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Brett works in a restaurant that has a vegetable garden. Part of his job is to trim the stems from, or prune, the tomato plants.</atomic>
<atomic>He wanted to know if pruning the plants affected how the tomatoes grew.</atomic>
<atomic>He thought that the plants he had pruned would produce larger tomatoes.</atomic>
<atomic>To test this, Brett pruned twelve of his tomato plants and left another twelve unpruned. Each week, he weighed the tomatoes that he picked.</atomic>
<atomic>After one month, he compared the average weight from each plant to see if tomatoes grew larger on the pruned plants.</atomic>
<atomic>His results showed that the pruned plants did have heavier tomatoes.</atomic>
<atomic>Brett presented his experiment and results to his coworkers, and they discussed his conclusions.</atomic>
<atomic>They decided to continue to prune all of the tomato plants.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Colin runs a catering business.</atomic>
<atomic>He wondered where he should chill sodas for an event: in the fridge, a cooler filled with ice water, or a cooler filled with ice cubes.</atomic>

<atomic>He recalled that solids conduct heat better than liquids or gases, so he reasoned that the fridge should be the least effective, and the cooler with solid ice should be the most effective.</atomic>

<atomic>To test his idea, Colin opened nine bottles of soda and measured their temperatures. He put three in the fridge, three in a cooler with ice water, and three in a cooler with ice cubes. He checked the sodas' temperatures every five minutes and compared them.</atomic>
<atomic>The sodas in the fridge cooled the slowest, as expected. But surprisingly, the sodas in the ice water cooled the fastest!</atomic>
<atomic>He realized that the solid ice did not touch the bottles' entire surface, while the ice water did.</atomic>
<atomic>Colin revised his prediction: Encasing the sodas in a block of ice would cool them the most effectively, but it was more practical to use ice water.</atomic>
<atomic>He shared his findings with his employees.</atomic>

<atomic>He recalled that solids conduct heat better than liquids or gases, so he reasoned that the fridge should be the least effective, and the cooler with solid ice should be the most effective.</atomic>

<atomic>To test his idea, Colin opened nine bottles of soda and measured their temperatures. He put three in the fridge, three in a cooler with ice water, and three in a cooler with ice cubes. He checked the sodas' temperatures every five minutes and compared them.</atomic>
<atomic>The sodas in the fridge cooled the slowest, as expected. But surprisingly, the sodas in the ice water cooled the fastest!</atomic>
<atomic>He realized that the solid ice did not touch the bottles' entire surface, while the ice water did.</atomic>
<atomic>Colin revised his prediction: Encasing the sodas in a block of ice would cool them the most effectively, but it was more practical to use ice water.</atomic>
<atomic>He shared his findings with his employees.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Martha had a stomachache one day, so her dad gave her a tablet of antacid dissolved in water. After she drank it, she asked him why he crushed the tablet before adding it to the water.</atomic>
<atomic>He told her that crushing the tablet speeds up the dissolving process.</atomic>

<atomic>She decided to see if he was right, so she set up an experiment using six cups of water and six antacid tablets. She added a whole tablet to three of the cups and a crushed tablet to the three remaining cups. She then measured how long each tablet took to dissolve completely.</atomic>
<atomic>She averaged the times for each set of three tablets and compared them.</atomic>
<atomic>Finding that the crushed tablets had dissolved quicker than the whole ones, she concluded that her dad was correct.</atomic>
<atomic>When her sister had a stomachache later, Martha told her about their dad's trick.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Shelley pushed Grace and Grace's little brother, Zack, on swings.</atomic>
<atomic>Shelley noticed that Zack always swung back in less time than Grace.</atomic>
<atomic>Shelley asked Grace if she thought the weight on a swing was related to the time it took to return.</atomic>
<atomic>To find out, Grace stood back four feet and released a swing three times, once with a light weight attached to it, once with a medium weight, and once with a heavy weight.</atomic>
<atomic>Shelley measured how long it took the swing to go forward and back each time.</atomic>
<atomic>They repeated the tests on ten swings.</atomic>
<atomic>They decided that weight on a swing wasn't related to swinging time, since for each swing the time was similar with all three weights.</atomic>
<atomic>Then, Shelley noticed that swings with shorter chains always swung back sooner.</atomic>
<atomic>She thought that chain length would determine swinging time and that shortening a swing's chains would shorten the time it took to swing back.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Rita grew roses for a flower shop. One day, she noticed tumor-like growths on her rose stems.</atomic>

<atomic>She read a book about plant diseases and learned that the plants had crown gall disease, which is caused by a type of bacteria. She also read that allicin, a chemical found in garlic, can kill bacteria.</atomic>
<atomic>She was curious if garlic could prevent more tumors from forming on her plants.</atomic>
<atomic>Rita sprayed garlic juice on ten infected plants and water on another ten.</atomic>
<atomic>After one month, she compared the number of new tumors on plants in each group and found no difference between them.</atomic>
<atomic>Rita thought that the concentration of allicin in her garlic spray might be too low, so spraying the plants with pure allicin would decrease the number of new tumors.</atomic>
<atomic>She repeated her experiment, this time spraying the plants with a solution of pure allicin.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Harry was playing with a rubber band and wondered how the stretchiness of flexible materials might vary.</atomic>
<atomic>Harry thought that rubber bands would stretch more than other common flexible materials, like plastic wrap or silicone, because they feel more elastic and springy.</atomic>

<atomic>Harry collected a few items: a rubber band, a piece of plastic wrap, and a silicone baking mat. He cut the rubber band to make a strip and then cut similarly sized pieces from the other items. He then gently pulled on the two ends of the rubber band until it reached its limit, and his sister measured its length. Harry and his sister repeated this with the other two materials.</atomic>
<atomic>They noticed that the rubber band stretched a lot, the plastic wrap stretched less, and the silicone mat stretched very little.</atomic>
<atomic>Harry determined that rubber is more elastic than plastic wrap and silicone, which allows it to stretch the most.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Olivia was getting ready to go for a hike. In order to stay hydrated, she dissolved an electrolyte tablet in a glass of water.</atomic>
<atomic>As she waited for the tablet to fully dissolve, she wondered how she could speed up the reaction rate.</atomic>
<atomic>Olivia predicted that warmer water would cause electrolyte tablets to dissolve more quickly.</atomic>

<atomic>She filled four cups with equal volumes of water. She warmed two of the cups in the microwave and left the other two cups at room temperature. She dropped one tablet into each cup at the same time and used a timer to track how long each tablet took to stop fizzing.</atomic>
<atomic>She averaged the times from each group and noticed that the warmer water almost cut the fizz time in half!</atomic>
<atomic>Olivia concluded that the temperature of the water does affect the reaction rate of electrolyte tablets.</atomic>
<atomic>She shared her results with her hiking group.</atomic>

<atomic>She read that cucumbers are sensitive to cold, so she wondered if using a heating pad would encourage her cucumber seeds to germinate faster.</atomic>
<atomic>She predicted that her cucumber seeds would germinate more quickly when kept at a higher temperature.</atomic>
<atomic>Pam planted six cucumber seeds in a planter that she kept on a heating pad and six in an identical planter left on the counter.</atomic>
<atomic>After one week, she found that the cucumber seeds in the planter on the heating pad had sprouted, while those left on the counter had not.</atomic>
<atomic>Pam concluded that cucumber seeds germinate more quickly when kept at warmer temperatures.</atomic>
<atomic>She shared her findings with her friends at the farmers' market.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>As Simon opened a can of soda, he remembered hearing that soft drinks are fizzy because there is carbon dioxide dissolved in them.</atomic>
<atomic>He knew that sugar and salt dissolve better in hot liquids, so he reasoned that hot soft drinks can dissolve more carbon dioxide and will therefore be fizzier.</atomic>

<atomic>So Simon got nine identical cans of soda. After opening them, he left three in the refrigerator, three on the kitchen counter, and three outside in the hot sun. Five hours later, he took a sip from each can.</atomic>
<atomic>To his surprise, the cold sodas were the fizziest, while the hot ones had gone flat!</atomic>
<atomic>Based on his experiment, Simon determined that cold soft drinks are fizzier than hot soft drinks.</atomic>
<atomic>He reasoned that gases, like carbon dioxide, must dissolve differently than solids, like salt and sugar.</atomic>
<atomic>At a cookout the next day, Simon told his friends to keep their sodas in the shade to help the sodas stay fizzy.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Brenda was coaching tennis on a hot summer day. As she hit a ball that had been left on the court, she was surprised to find that it bounced more than the brand new ones she had just opened!</atomic>

<atomic>She thought that it must have something to do with the ball's temperature—the hot asphalt must have warmed it up and made it bouncier than the new ones that had been in an air-conditioned house.</atomic>

<atomic>To test the idea, Brenda and her friend gathered nine new tennis balls. They put three in the freezer, left three in the hot sun, and left the remaining three on the kitchen table at room temperature. Thirty minutes later, Brenda took all the balls and dropped each one from the top of a 10-foot ladder. Her friend measured how high each one bounced.</atomic>
<atomic>They found that the heated tennis balls bounced the highest, while the frozen ones bounced the lowest.</atomic>
<atomic>They concluded that tennis balls must become bouncier as their temperature rises.</atomic>
<atomic>The next day, Brenda shared what she learned with her fellow coaches.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Devin learned in science class that oil and water do not mix together. His teacher proved this by adding both substances to a container and shaking it. Devin noticed that the oil floated to the top of the container after it had sat untouched for a while.</atomic>
<atomic>He wondered, "Could a thick enough oil layer prevent the water from evaporating?"</atomic>
<atomic>He guessed that the thicker the oil layer was, the less water would evaporate because the oil would act as a barrier and stop water molecules from escaping into the air.</atomic>

<atomic>Devin set up nine identical cups and filled each one with an equal amount of water. In the first three cups, he added a thin layer of vegetable oil, just enough to cover the surface. In the next three cups, he added a thicker layer of oil. He did not add any oil to the remaining cups. He left them all on the counter for three days. Then Devin measured the water level in each cup and calculated the average for each group.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that the water level was the lowest in the cup with no oil and the highest in the cup with a thick layer of oil.</atomic>
<atomic>He concluded that a thicker layer of oil does indeed reduce water evaporation more effectively than a thin layer.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Hannah's friends followed the "five-second rule": they would eat food that had dropped on the floor, but only if it was on the floor for less than five seconds.</atomic>
<atomic>Hannah thought that bacteria would stick to food as soon as it touched the floor, so the amount of time on the floor wouldn't affect how much bacteria stuck to the food.</atomic>

<atomic>She placed twelve boiled noodles on the kitchen floor, picked up six after three seconds, and picked up the rest after ten seconds. Then, she touched each noodle to a separate Petri dish used to grow bacteria.</atomic>
<atomic>After one week, the bacteria that had transferred from each noodle to its Petri dish had grown to visible clusters.</atomic>

<atomic>Because there were more bacteria on the ten-second dishes than the three-second dishes, Hannah reasoned that the amount of time on the floor did affect how much bacteria stuck to the food.</atomic>
<atomic>She showed her friends pictures of the Petri dishes and a graph of her results.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Sofia loves making lemonade with fresh-squeezed lemon juice and water. She noticed that after a day or two in the fridge, her lemonade would turn brown and lose its fresh taste.</atomic>

<atomic>While looking at the ingredient list on a store-bought lemonade bottle, she saw that it included sugar and citric acid. Sofia wondered if adding these ingredients to her homemade lemonade would help preserve its color and freshness.</atomic>

<atomic>To test this idea, Sofia prepared six identical bottles of freshly squeezed lemon juice from the same batch. She added one teaspoon of sugar to two of the bottles and one teaspoon of powdered citric acid to the next two. She added nothing to the remaining bottles. Then she labeled the bottles and placed them in the fridge.</atomic>
<atomic>After three days, she observed that the bottles with plain lemon juice and the ones with sugar had all turned brown, while the ones with citric acid stayed bright and fresh.</atomic>
<atomic>Sofia now predicted that citric acid was more effective than sugar at preserving lemonade's color and freshness.</atomic>

elements.text: Grace's brother thought that crushed ice would keep his soda cooler than whole ice cubes.

elements.text: Hassan grew ten mint plants on his back porch. He grew each plant in its own pot, and each pot was the same size and shape. Two months later, Hassan counted the number of leaves on each of the ten plants. He compared the number of leaves on the plants in each group.

elements.text: Emir designed an electric circuit to test how well different types of metal conduct electricity. elements.text: Akira was using steel to make rusted sculptures. After building each sculpture, she caused the steel in the sculpture to rust by placing it into a tub filled with salt water for eight hours. Akira wondered if steel would rust faster submerged in vinegar instead of salt water.

mainText.text: Vivian applied a thin layer of wax to the underside of her snowboard and rode the board straight down a hill. Then, she removed the wax and rode the snowboard straight down the hill again. She repeated the rides four more times, alternating whether she rode with a thin layer of wax on the board or not. Her friend Bryce timed each ride. Vivian and Bryce calculated the average time it took to slide straight down the hill on the snowboard with wax compared to the average time on the snowboard without wax.

lessons.name: Understand an experimental protocol about plant growth

pieces.text: The instructions for how to carry out a science experiment can be found in an

. An experimental protocol often includes the list of materials you need for the experiment. The protocol also includes the procedure, which is a list of steps for carrying out the experiment. Some experimental protocols include data tables for recording the results of the experiment.

header.text: The experimental protocol below is for an experiment investigating tomato plant growth. Read through the experimental protocol, then answer the question below.

elements.text: Pour the soil into the large plastic container and add water until the soil is moist.
Fill the pots with the moistened soil. Label each pot with a number from 1 through 10.
Plant one tomato plant in each pot.
In pots 6 through 10, add two earthworms just beneath the soil surface.
Place all of the pots next to each other in a warm, sunny area.
Once a day, give each plant four ounces of water.
After three months, count the number of tomatoes on each plant.
Record your results in the following tables.

Plants grown in soil with earthworms

header.text: The experimental protocol below is for an experiment investigating pepper plant growth. Read through the experimental protocol, then answer the question below.

elements.text: Pour the soil into the large plastic container and add water until the soil is moist.
Fill each pot with moistened soil. Label each pot with a number from 1 through 10.
Plant one pepper plant in each pot.
In pots 6 through 10, mix one teaspoon of controlled-release fertilizer into the top two inches of soil.
Place all of the pots next to each other in a warm, sunny area.
Once a day, give each plant four ounces of water.
After three months, count the number of peppers on each plant.
Record your results in the following tables.

contents.text: In this experiment, the independent variable is the amount of time each beaker is under a heat lamp. The amount of time spent under a heat lamp may affect the rate of evaporation, or how quickly the water evaporates.
The more quickly the water evaporates, the less water will be remaining after three days. The water remaining after three days is the dependent variable.

content.text: Does the amount of time under a heat lamp affect the rate of evaporation?

content.text: Does the salinity of water affect the rate of evaporation?

content.text: Does the amount of time under a heat lamp affect the water temperature?

explanationText.text: In this experiment, beakers are heated by heat lamps for different amounts of time. However, data on water temperature are not collected or recorded. So, this experiment does not test the effect of time under a heat lamp on water temperature.

contents.text: In this experiment, the independent variable is the salinity of the water. The salinity of the water may affect the rate of evaporation, or how quickly the water evaporates.
The more quickly the water evaporates, the less water will remain after three days. The water remaining after three days is the dependent variable.

header.text: So, the experiment can answer this question:

content.text: Does the salinity of the water affect the rate of evaporation?

header.text: The experiment cannot answer these questions:

content.text: Does the size of the beaker affect the rate of evaporation?

explanationText.text: In this experiment, the beakers are identical, or the same. So, this experiment does not test the effect of using beakers of different sizes.

content.text: Does the temperature of the water affect the rate of evaporation?

explanationText.text: In this experiment, the temperature of the water in each beaker is the same. So, this experiment does not test the effect of temperature.
